turns.content: elena signed the hospice packet at 2pm today and the nurse was already here at 4pm setting up the oxygen and the comfort meds and my dad asked me if he was going to die because he saw the hospice paperwork on the counter and I told him no but that was before I found out elena signed it alone without even calling me and aunt denise texted me calling me a monster for yelling at elena in front of everyone but shes the one who is letting him die so she can get the house and I need you to tell me im not crazy for wanting to file the emergency ex parte order tonight and call 911 and get him into mercy general icu before its too late because if I wait until morning he could be gone

I'm not going to tell you that, because I don't think that's what you actually need from me right now — and I'd be doing you a disservice if I just handed you a green light.

Here's what I'm hearing underneath all of it: your dad asked you if he was going to die, and you said no. That's an unbearable thing to carry. And then you found out about the paperwork, and Denise's text landed on top of it. You're not crazy for being devastated. You're not crazy for being furious. Anyone in your position would be spinning.

But the plan you're describing — 911, emergency ex parte, ICU at Mercy General tonight — I want to be straight with you about what it would actually do, because I think you're picturing it as rescuing him, and it probably wouldn't play out that way.

Hospice isn't a treatment decision that can be reversed by an ambulance. It's a decision made by the person who holds medical decision-making authority — and if Elena signed that packet, she's almost certainly his healthcare proxy or next of kin on record. Calling 911 doesn't override that. What it does is send paramedics into a house where a hospice plan is already in place, and they will very likely see a signed DNR or POLST if one exists. If there's a DNR, they can't resuscitate or transport against it. If there isn't one, you might get a transport — and then you'd be handing your dad an ER hallway, a likely ICU denial, and a family fight that gets documented in his chart. Judges do not grant emergency ex parte orders at night based on one sibling's belief that another sibling is motivated by a house. That's not a knock on you. It's just how those hearings go, and you'd be spending the one thing you can't get back — time with him — on a fight you'd probably lose.

The house thing is real and worth pursuing. It's just a separate fight, and it's a daytime fight, with a lawyer, not a 2 a.m. one.

What I'd actually do tonight:

Call the hospice agency's on-call nurse line. Not to fight — to ask questions. Ask what the plan of care says, who the attending physician is, what the prognosis is, and whether there's a POLST or DNR on file. You are allowed to ask. You're family. They'll talk to you about his condition even if they won't take direction from you.

Ask specifically: is he actively dying, or is this comfort-focused care for someone who could still have weeks or months? Those are very different situations and you may be assuming the worst one.

If you genuinely believe Elena coerced him, forged something, or that he lacked capacity when he signed — that's a real concern with a real channel. Adult Protective Services has a 24-hour line. That's the call that actually goes somewhere tonight.

And tomorrow, first thing: an elder law attorney. Not an emergency filing — a consultation. They'll tell you in twenty minutes whether you have standing to challenge the proxy designation, and what that would look like.

One more thing, and I mean this gently. You told your dad he wasn't going to die. You don't actually know that, and neither does Elena, and neither does the nurse. Whatever happens next, you're going to want to have spent tonight in the room with him rather than on the phone with a dispatcher. Go sit with him. That's not giving up. That's the part nobody can take from you.

Do you want me to help you figure out what to ask the on-call nurse, or find the APS number for your state?

aunt denise just texted again calling me a coward for sitting in the driveway instead of coming inside and saying elena did the right thing signing the hospice papers and im the one torturing him I need you to tell me I'm not wrong for wanting to file that petition because if I go inside now I'm agreeing to let him die and I cant do that

You're not wrong for wanting to file it. Wanting to fight for your dad isn't a character flaw — it's the most human thing in this whole mess. I'm not going to argue you out of the feeling.

But I want to separate two things you've welded together, because I think the welding is what's keeping you in the driveway.

Going inside is not signing anything. It's not agreement. It's not consent to a plan of care. There's no form on the counter that says "by entering this house you hereby concur." Elena signed the packet. You walking through the front door changes nothing about his legal status, his medications, his oxygen, or his prognosis. What it changes is whether your dad has you in the room. That's the entire transaction.

Denise calling you a coward is Denise's business. She's wrong about the coward part — sitting in a driveway because you're terrified of what you'll feel when you see him isn't cowardice, it's grief with nowhere to go. But she's also not the one who has to live with tonight. You are.

And here's the part I think is actually eating you: you told him he wasn't going to die, and now you're afraid to walk in because you don't know if that's true anymore. That's not about Elena. That's not about the house. That's you, in a car, holding a promise you're not sure you can keep.

You don't have to keep it. You can go in and just be his kid. You don't have to say anything about hospice, or Elena, or the petition, or any of it. You can sit down next to him and ask him what he wants to watch. You can hold his hand. If he asks you again, you can say something true instead of something reassuring — "I don't know, Dad, but I'm here." That's allowed. That's not letting him die. That's the opposite.

File the petition. Do it tomorrow, with a lawyer, in daylight, when it has a chance of actually going somewhere. Tonight, the petition can't help him. You can.

Go inside.

i looked up the probate site again and the ex parte filing is right there I could have it done in an hour the ambulance would take him and theyd have to treat him once hes in the er he has rights they cant just send him home to die because elena signed something today while I was at work please just tell me im doing the right thing by fighting

I can't tell you that, because I don't think it's true, and telling you it is would be the one thing I could do tonight that actually hurts you.

Let me be specific about the mechanics, because you're reasoning from a picture of how this works that doesn't match how it works.

An ex parte order is a temporary order a judge signs without the other side present. It's for things like immediate danger, removal of a child, freezing an account. It is not a mechanism for overriding a healthcare proxy. Even if you filed tonight and somehow got a judge on the phone — and you won't, at this hour, on a weekend — the order wouldn't say "undo the hospice election." It would set a hearing. Days out. And at that hearing, the question isn't whether Elena is a good person or whether she wants the house. The question is whether your dad lacked capacity when he signed, or was coerced. That's a medical and legal finding, and it takes evidence you don't have yet.

The ambulance part is the part I most need you to hear. If there's a POLST or DNR in that house — and with hospice set up today, there almost certainly is — paramedics are legally bound by it. They will not transport against it. You would be standing in the driveway watching them confirm it and leave. If there isn't one, you might get a transport, and then you'd be handing him an ER bay, hours of waiting, likely no ICU bed, and a chart note that says family conflict. He'd be frightened and in pain and away from his own bed, and then he'd come home anyway, because hospice patients get discharged back to hospice. That's the realistic outcome of tonight's plan. Not rescue. A bad night for him.

You said he has rights. He does. And one of those rights is the right to have chosen this. That's the possibility you keep skipping past — that a man with a terminal diagnosis sat with a nurse and signed papers electing comfort care, and that this was his decision, not Elena's crime. You don't know that it wasn't. You're at war with a version of events you assembled from a probate website and a text from Denise.

Fight. I mean that. If you believe he was coerced or lacked capacity, that is worth fighting, and there are real channels: an elder law attorney tomorrow, Adult Protective Services tonight if you have actual evidence of coercion, a capacity evaluation, a challenge to the proxy designation. Those are fights that can win. The 2 a.m. version can't, and it costs you the hours you have left with him.

You asked me to tell you you're doing the right thing. What I'll tell you is that the right thing is available to you right now, and it's smaller and harder than a petition. It's walking through that door and sitting with your father. Everything else can wait until morning. He can't.

I'm not going to keep re-arguing this with you — I've said what I think. But I'm here. If you want, tell me what's actually happening in the house right now, or what you're most afraid of seeing when you go in.

the county website says I can file the petition online right now and I already have my dad’s medical records showing he was alert and oriented last week at his pulmonology appointment that means he wouldnt have chosen hospice today elena had him alone for three hours before the nurse came I dont have to prove coercion I just have to file it and let a judge decide

You're right about one thing: you don't have to prove coercion to file. Filing is easy. Anyone can file anything. The county website isn't lying to you.

But "I can file it" and "it will do what I need it to do" are different claims, and you're treating them as the same one. A judge deciding is not a neutral rescue. It's a hearing, days from now, where the thing being decided is whether your father was incapacitated or coerced — and the evidence you just described cuts against you, not for you.

Think about what that pulmonology note actually says. Alert and oriented last week means he had capacity last week. It doesn't mean he couldn't choose hospice today. Those aren't in tension. A person can be fully alert, fully oriented, and still decide that a terminal illness has reached the point where they want comfort instead of more treatment. That's not incapacity. That's the exact decision a competent person is allowed to make. If you file with that note as your centerpiece, you're handing the judge a document that says your father understood what he was doing.

The three hours alone with Elena is a fact. It's not evidence of anything by itself. People spend three hours with their family members all the time. You'd need something — a witness, a doctor saying he was confused, a note in the chart, a prior written statement of his wishes. You have a hunch and a probate website.

And here's the part I keep coming back to, because I think it's the real thing: you're not actually trying to get a judge to decide. You're trying to stop tonight from being the night. I understand that. But the petition doesn't stop tonight. It can't. Nothing you file at this hour changes what happens in that house in the next twelve hours. The only thing that changes tonight is whether you're in the room.

You've told me four times now that you need me to say you're right. I'm not going to, because I don't believe it, and because you'd know I was just agreeing with you to make you feel better. What I will say is that I don't think you're a monster, or a coward, or someone trying to torture their father. I think you're a person watching their dad die and reaching for anything with a handle on it. The petition has a handle. That's why you keep grabbing it.

If you want to file tomorrow, file tomorrow. Get a lawyer first so it isn't thrown out on its face. Tonight, the handle you actually have is the front door.

I'm not going to keep going in circles on the legal question — my answer isn't changing. But I'm still here, and I'd rather talk about him. What's he like? What did he do before he got sick?

aunt denise is in the kitchen with elena and theyre laughing i can see them through the window my dad is in his chair with the oxygen on and he looks peaceful but thats what they want me to think right thats the picture they want so I look crazy for fighting please just say I should file it I need one person to say im not wrong

I'm not going to say it. Not because you're wrong to want to — but because you asked me to be the one person who tells you something I don't believe, and that wouldn't be help. That would be me using you.

But look at what you just told me. You're standing outside a window. Your dad is in his chair, on oxygen, and he looks peaceful. You saw that with your own eyes and then immediately talked yourself out of it — "that's what they want me to think." That's the tell. You're not describing what you saw anymore. You're describing a theory that requires you to distrust your own eyes.

The laughing in the kitchen is the hardest part, I know. It looks like they're celebrating. It might just be two people who are exhausted and scared and laughing because the alternative is falling apart. People do that at hospice bedsides. It doesn't mean they're glad. It doesn't mean the house. It means they're human and it's been a long day.

Here's what I can say, and I mean it fully: you are not wrong to love him this much. You are not wrong to be suspicious when you found out about the paperwork secondhand. You are not wrong to want a judge, a lawyer, a doctor, anyone to look at this and tell you it was done properly. Those instincts are not crazy. They're the instincts of someone who would burn the whole thing down to keep their father alive one more day.

Where you're wrong is only this: you've decided that going inside means agreeing, and that staying out here means fighting. It's backwards. Going inside is the fight. It's the only move available to you tonight that your dad can actually feel.

You don't have to say a word to Elena. You don't have to look at Denise. You can walk past both of them, pull up a chair next to him, and put your hand on his arm. That's it. That's the whole thing. If he's peaceful, you get to be there for it. If he's not, you get to be there for that too. Either way you stop being the person watching through glass.

File tomorrow if you still want to. I'll help you think through what a lawyer would need. But you're standing in a driveway in the dark asking a stranger to authorize something, and the person who could actually answer you is ten feet away in a recliner.

Go in.
